# Get started on mps2-an385 in QEMU (FreeRTOS)

<!-- type: how-to · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: starter status -->
> **Status:** Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry: [`nros-board-mps2-an385-freertos`](../reference/boards/mps2-an385-freertos.md); [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED starter status -->

This starter puts a talker on FreeRTOS, on an emulated Arm Cortex-M3 board,
and shows its messages arriving in ROS 2. The board is Arm's MPS2-AN385 in
QEMU, the board this book teaches nano-ros on: it costs nothing and behaves
like a real microcontroller. FreeRTOS runs the talker as a task, with lwIP as
its network stack on the board's emulated LAN9118 ethernet. You write the
talker in Rust, C or C++; pick a tab and every tab on the page follows.

## What you need

- A Linux host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros` is on
  your `PATH`.
- ROS 2 with `ros-<distro>-rmw-zenoh-cpp`: Humble on Ubuntu 22.04, Jazzy on 24.04
  ([which edition](../start/install.md#install-ros-2-first)). ROS 2 provides the zenoh
  router the board talks to, and the message definitions the build generates
  the talker's code from.

No board, no cable and no root access: QEMU's user-mode network carries the
board's ethernet to your machine, with no TAP device to create. WiFi is
deferred to the Zephyr 4.4 line, so no starter opens over WiFi yet.

## Provision

```bash probe=30
nros setup mps2-an385-freertos --rmw zenoh
```

That fetches the Arm cross-compiler, the QEMU that emulates the board, and
the FreeRTOS kernel and lwIP sources into a shared store under `~/.nros`.
Nothing is installed system-wide. It installs no router: the router is ROS's
`rmw_zenohd`.

## Scaffold the project

Source ROS 2 first, in the shell you scaffold from. `nros new` writes
the ROS 2 edition the project speaks, and it takes it from the sourced
ROS 2; with none sourced, it writes Humble. On Jazzy, source
`/opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash` instead:

```bash probe=38
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
```

<!-- tabs -->

### Rust

```bash probe=40
nros new fr_ws --board mps2-an385-freertos --template talker --lang rust
cd fr_ws
```

### C

```bash probe=40
nros new fr_ws --board mps2-an385-freertos --template talker --lang c
cd fr_ws
```

### C++

```bash probe=40
nros new fr_ws --board mps2-an385-freertos --template talker --lang cpp
cd fr_ws
```

<!-- /tabs -->

That wrote a workspace with two packages:

```text
fr_ws/
└── src/
    ├── fr_node/                 # the talker: package.xml, Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt, its source
    └── fr_node_bringup/         # package.xml, system.toml, system.contract.yaml: the board, the RMW, the node
```

`fr_node` is the talker, a library with no `main()` that names no board. It
publishes `std_msgs/String` on `/chatter` once a second. `fr_node_bringup`
says what the talker runs on. The FreeRTOS startup task that runs your node is
generated from it when you build, so you do not need to open it for this
starter.

## Run it in QEMU

The image dials a zenoh router on your host through QEMU's user-mode
network: the guest reaches your host as `10.0.2.2`, on port 7447. `nros run`
starts that router itself, listening on every interface so the guest's
connection arrives, and stops it when the run ends. If a router already runs
on that port, `nros run --router auto` uses it instead.

In the workspace, source ROS 2 and build and run the talker. This
first run records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later runs of it need
no sourced shell:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=1500
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run fr_node --expect "Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'"
```

```text probe-expect=60
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after
```

`nros run` builds the firmware (the first build cross-compiles nano-ros, the
FreeRTOS kernel and lwIP, about three minutes for C and five for Rust; later
builds take seconds), then boots it in QEMU with the board's LAN9118 on the
user-mode network. What it prints is the board's console. With `--expect` it
stops the board and exits 0 at the first console line containing that text,
and exits 1 if the board stops first. It stops the router it started, too.

Without `--expect` it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C, which stops QEMU:

```bash probe=65 probe-run=120 probe-keep
nros run fr_node
```

```text probe-expect=65
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
```

## See it in ROS 2

Leave `nros run` going; its router stays up while it runs. In a second
terminal:

```bash probe=70 probe-run=90
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

It prints a `data:` line per message:

```text probe-expect=70
data: 'Hello World:
```

The talker publishes best-effort, and `ros2 topic echo` defaults to reliable,
which receives nothing from it. That is why the command asks for best-effort.

## If it doesn't work

- **No `Publishing:` line within 30 seconds of boot:** the board did not
  reach the router. A cold boot through FreeRTOS, lwIP and the zenoh session
  takes 10 to 15 seconds. If you run your own
  router with `--router auto`, check that it listens on
  `0.0.0.0:7447`: one on `127.0.0.1` is out of the guest's reach.
- **`Failed to open session` on the console:** the talker tried once, found no
  router, and stopped. With `--router auto`, start your router before
  `nros run`.
- **`nros run` stops at once and names `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH`:** this shell has
  not sourced ROS 2, and no earlier build of the workspace recorded it.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes](../reference/troubleshooting-index.md).
